subject: Agriculture
title: Mendel's Pea Revolution
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mendel's Pea Revolution.

hook.text: Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of inheritance in a monastery garden. Nobody noticed for 35 years.

buildup.text: Mendel crossed pea plants and tracked traits across generations—tall vs short, wrinkled vs smooth.

discovery.text: He found traits followed mathematical ratios—3:1 in the second generation. Heredity had rules.

twist.text: His 1866 paper was ignored. Only after 1900, when three scientists independently rediscovered his laws, did genetics begin.

climax.text: Mendel's principles underpin all modern plant breeding—from hybrid corn to CRISPR-edited crops.

punchline.text: A monk with peas invented genetics. The world took 35 years to notice.

quiz.question: Why was Mendel's work not recognized until 1900?
options: His 1866 paper was published obscurely and ignored for 35 years

details.summary: Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants in the 1860s laid the foundation for modern genetics and crop breeding. This topic covers his laws of inheritance, their rediscovery decades later, and how Mendelian genetics transformed plant improvement forever.
details.whyItMatters: Mendel's laws of inheritance gave plant breeders a scientific framework to predict and select desirable traits, replacing millennia of trial-and-error selection with targeted breeding strategies.
takeaways: Mendel identified dominant and recessive traits by crossing thousands of pea plants
His work was ignored for 35 years before being independently rediscovered in 1900
Mendelian genetics made it possible to breed crops for specific traits systematically

faq.question: What did Mendel discover from his pea plant experiments?
faq.answer: Mendel discovered that traits are inherited as discrete units (now called genes) following predictable ratios. He established the laws of segregation and independent assortment, showing that offspring inherit one allele from each parent.

faq.question: How did Mendel's genetics change agriculture?
faq.answer: Mendel's laws gave breeders the ability to predict outcomes of crosses and systematically select for traits like yield, disease resistance, and quality. This scientific approach replaced random selection and accelerated crop improvement dramatically.
